1oqtwoj:596: While almost all the spotlight of AI Coding is on the frontend and client side—generating a page, writing an app—an important question seems to have been avoided: Can AI write code in backend systems that truly “blow up” when something goes wrong? Tencent CDN LEGO is exactly such a system. With 1 million lines of core code and 3 million lines of deeply modified third-party libraries, it serves hundreds of millions of users and carries critical responsibilities such as traffic scheduling, protocol parsing, security protection, and cache acceleration. What it faces is not deterministic input-output, but uncontrollable clients, uncontrollable origin servers, multiple protocols, multiple configurations, and the full public-network attack surface—the stacking of these dimensions is not simple addition but multiplicative complexity explosion, with the theoretical combined paths reaching as many as 13,824 × N. Having AI write code in such a complex system means a single line of error could become a network-wide incident. But precisely because it is hard, it is worth doing. We systematically explored the landing path for AI Coding in high-risk backend scenarios: on one hand, we used AI with zero human-written code to implement a Rust version of the Nonstop proxy framework, thereby probing the boundaries and behavioral characteristics of AI coding; on the other hand, in the ultra-large-scale C++ LEGO project, we built a five-layer Harness Engineering architecture and multi-model adversarial CR, establishing a complete quality barrier for every line of AI-produced code from generation to production. This article is not only a practical record of introducing AI Coding into the Tencent CDN core framework, but also a complete engineering path from “AI can write” to “AI-written code is safe to use.”

The functional boundaries we were familiar with are loosening.  
Junior development: no longer just an executor who types code, but evolves into an operator who can harness AI to write code; mastering Skills and Prompts becomes a new basic skill.  
Senior development: upgraded to Harness Engineer, whose core work is designing AI’s constraints, context, and rules, allowing AI to run efficiently on a controlled track.  
Architect: focus shifts from system design to human-AI collaboration architecture; true judgment lies in deciding “what to hand to AI and what must be controlled by humans.”  
Testing and security engineers: evolve into AI Quality Engineer and AI Security Expert respectively—the former designs test closed loops to verify AI output; the latter builds AI security testing Skills and includes computational security considerations.

e8mv4z:404: Multi-model, multi-agent adversarial CR is one of the most original engineering innovations in this article. Its core idea (lines 351-387) can be summarized as: using multiple models to independently review in parallel, then cross-validating, to uncover single-model knowledge blind spots, attention blind spots, and confirmation bias. The effectiveness of adversarial CR comes from an insight rooted in information theory: when multiple independent "experts" review the same code, the sets of issues each one misses are often non-overlapping. Through cross-validation, issues discovered by multiple models at the same time have high confidence, while issues found by only a single model need to enter a debate-style discussion stage. This mechanism essentially simulates the cross-review process among human engineers. However, the article also candidly acknowledges its limitation: a false-positive rate as high as 36% (line 465)—that is, among 9 code issues, only 1 is a true P0. This means that although adversarial CR improves defect discovery, it also adds significant review burden. The 36% false-positive rate may be related to the original design intent of adversarial CR—preferring to over-report rather than miss real risks. This is a classic engineering trade-off between "rather cry wolf than miss" and "rather miss than cry wolf."

During the actual application of AI Coding in the project, we also found many problems. Based on 57 real cases, we conducted in-depth analysis and distilled them into 13 typical problem types and 5 root causes, establishing a systematic problem-awareness framework as well as corresponding prevention and response mechanisms. Problem list: These problems recurred repeatedly in our actual projects; building this problem list helps us identify and avoid these risks early when using AI Coding. No. | Problem Type | Severity | Source
---|---|---|---
1 | Async semantic misuse (blocking send in tokio) | Critical | nonstop
2 | Hallucination (calling/configuring non-existent APIs) | High | Both projects
3 | Incomplete changes (insert without cleanup) | High | Both projects
4 | Config detached from implementation | High | nonstop
5 | Security blind spots (timing attack/SSRF/JWT) | Critical | nonstop
6 | Flaky tests (platform differences) | Medium | nonstop
7 | Memory leak (DashMap only grows, never shrinks) | Critical | nonstop
8 | Incomplete protocol implementation | Critical | nonstop
9 | Modifying upper layers without reading lower layers | High | LEGO
10 | Source code analysis replacing actual testing | High | LEGO
11 | Large file edit corruption | Medium | nonstop
12 | Environment blind spots | Medium | LEGO
13 | Not saying "I don't know" | Highest | LEGO

Based on the above analysis, the common problems of AI Coding in large projects mainly stem from: ● Not saying "I don't know": this is the highest risk — AI outputs wrong conclusions with a confident tone, which instead lowers people's willingness to review ● Hallucination: fabricating function signatures, RFC section numbers, and percentage data ● Incomplete changes: local modifications while forgetting global impact (inserted but no cleanup) ● Pattern matching instead of verification: inferring identical behavior from similar code and skipping actual testing ● Lack of environment awareness: not distinguishing container/host, guessing directly without checking configuration. Root cause: AI lacks "uncertainty awareness" and "global perspective." So next, we need to address these two problems in a targeted way.
